ex.am: Before calculating, write down what you are given (mass, moles, or particle count) and what you need, then choose n = m/M or n times Avogadro's number to connect them.
ex.core:
- You cannot count atoms directly, so n = m/M bridges a measurable mass to moles.
- Avogadro's number (6.022x10^23/mol) bridges moles to particle count.
- A substance's molar mass in grams numerically equals one particle's average mass in amu.
ex.cpl: Using the wrong molar mass, such as an element's molar mass in a compound problem, or miscounting atoms when summing a compound's molar mass from its formula.
ex.hp:
1. Apply n = m/M (or a rearrangement) with the molar mass of the substance actually asked about.
2. Decide whether Avogadro's number is needed to reach a particle count.
3. Do not stop at moles when particles were requested.
ex.pb: Go to practice and, on every moles question, check which conversion you actually need first -- mass-to-moles uses molar mass, moles-to-particles uses Avogadro's number -- before doing any arithmetic.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Write what you are given and what you need, then link them with n = m/M or n times Avogadro's number.
How points are lost: Using the wrong molar mass, or miscounting atoms when summing a compound's molar mass.
ex.title: Moles and Molar Mass
ex.wsu:
- Stoichiometry, solution concentration and gas laws all start by converting between mass and moles.
- A wrong molar mass or a mole/particle mix-up propagates into every later calculation, not just this topic's.

ex.am: For each peak, multiply the isotope mass by its fractional abundance, then add the products across every peak to get the weighted average atomic mass.
ex.core:
- A single-element mass spectrum has one peak per isotope: position is the isotope's mass, size is its natural relative abundance.
- Average atomic mass is the isotope-weighted average of those peaks.
- Excluded from the AP Exam: spectra of multiple elements, or peaks from anything other than singly charged monatomic ions.
ex.cpl: Attributing isotope mass differences to electrons or protons instead of neutrons.
ex.hp:
1. Read each peak's mass and relative abundance.
2. Multiply mass by fractional abundance and sum across every peak.
3. To explain a mass difference, name neutron count: proton count (and electron count in a neutral atom) is fixed.
ex.pb: Return to practice and, on every mass-spectrum question, remember the isotope-mass story is always about neutrons -- and that multi-element spectra are outside what the AP Exam will ever ask you to interpret.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Multiply each isotope's mass by its fractional abundance, then add the products across every peak.
How points are lost: Attributing isotope mass differences to electrons or protons instead of neutrons.
ex.title: Mass Spectra of Elements
ex.wsu:
- This is how average atomic mass is actually measured, not memorized.
- Isotopes of one element share a proton count and differ only in neutron count.
- The 2025 FRQ isotope-mass-difference point scored a mean of just 0.55/1.0, mostly from attributing the difference to electrons or protons instead of neutrons.

ex.am: Assume a 100 g sample so mass percent becomes grams, convert each element's grams to moles, divide every mole value by the smallest mole value, then scale to whole numbers.
ex.core:
- Law of definite proportions: the mass ratio of elements in any pure sample of a compound is fixed.
- The empirical formula is the lowest whole-number atom ratio matching that mass ratio.
- A molecular formula is an integer multiple of it: actual molar mass divided by the empirical formula's mass.
ex.cpl: Stopping at the empirical formula when the molecular formula was asked for, by not scaling the empirical formula using the ratio of given molar mass to empirical formula mass.
ex.hp:
1. Convert given masses or mass percentages to moles of each element.
2. Divide every mole value by the smallest to get a whole-number ratio (the empirical formula).
3. Divide the molecular molar mass by the empirical formula's mass to find the scaling factor.
ex.pb: Head back to practice and, whenever a molar mass is given alongside percent composition, treat that as a signal the question wants the molecular formula, not just the empirical one.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Assume 100 g, convert grams to moles, divide by the smallest mole value, then scale to whole numbers.
How points are lost: Stopping at the empirical formula when the molecular formula was asked for.
ex.title: Elemental Composition of Pure Substances
ex.wsu:
- Experimental mass data, like combustion analysis (masses of CO2 and H2O from burning a sample), leads to a compound's formula.
- It works only because every sample of a pure compound gives the same element ratio, however much you burn.

ex.am: Compare the calculated mass ratio of components across two or more samples of the same material. A constant ratio supports a pure substance; a changing ratio supports a mixture.
ex.core:
- A pure substance has one particle type in a fixed proportion; a mixture has two or more whose proportions can vary sample to sample.
- A homogeneous mixture can look as uniform as a compound, so appearance never substitutes for checking whether the composition ratio stays constant across independent samples.
ex.cpl: Assuming a sample is a pure substance just because it looks uniform or homogeneous, instead of checking whether its elemental composition ratio stays constant across independent samples.
ex.hp:
1. Use elemental analysis data from two or more samples to test whether a component's mass ratio holds constant.
2. State a purity conclusion that follows from that comparison.
3. Do not rely on appearance, texture, or one sample's data.
ex.pb: Go to practice and, on every purity question, compare the actual calculated element ratios across samples first -- never decide purity from how a substance looks.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Compare the mass ratio of components across samples: a constant ratio supports a pure substance, a changing ratio supports a mixture.
How points are lost: Assuming a sample is pure because it looks uniform, without checking whether its composition ratio stays constant.
ex.title: Composition of Mixtures
ex.wsu:
- Fixed versus variable ratio is what makes empirical-formula reasoning (Topic 1.3) valid at all.
- The same evidence, a constant or inconstant elemental composition ratio, is what Unit 3's mixture-separation topics build on.

ex.am: Fill subshells in order of increasing energy (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, and so on), then explain any related property, such as ionization energy, using nuclear charge and electron distance or shielding rather than stopping at the configuration itself.
ex.core:
- An atom is a nucleus (protons and neutrons) with electrons around it.
- Coulomb's law: the pull between charges grows with the charges and shrinks with distance, F proportional to q1q2/r^2.
- Configuration notation and Aufbau filling order are tested; assigning n, l, ml, ms to single electrons is not.
ex.cpl: Writing a correct electron configuration but then explaining a related property, such as ionization energy, with a vague label like periodic trend instead of grounding the explanation in nuclear charge and electron distance or shielding, which is what the Coulomb's law reasoning actually requires.
ex.hp:
1. Write the ground-state configuration in Aufbau order.
2. Compare the two atoms on nuclear charge and on shell and shielding.
3. State the Coulomb's law result: stronger attraction, so more energy to remove an electron.
ex.pb: Return to practice and, whenever you compare two atoms' ionization energy or radius, name the specific Coulomb's-law factor that differs between them -- never stop at restating the trend's direction.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Fill subshells in order of increasing energy, then explain ionization energy through nuclear charge, distance and shielding.
How points are lost: Explaining a related property with a vague label like "periodic trend" after a correct configuration.
Remember it: Diagonal rule: write subshells in rows by shell number, then follow diagonals from upper right to lower left.
ex.title: Atomic Structure and Electron Configuration
ex.wsu:
- A correct configuration earns the reasoning point only when it is tied to nuclear charge and electron distance or shielding.
- "Periodic trend" names a pattern; it does not explain one.
- Topic 1.6 reads these same configurations as photoelectron spectra.

ex.am: Count the number of peaks and compare their relative heights first to identify subshell electron counts, then match that pattern to a specific element's electron configuration before discussing binding energy.
ex.core:
- Each PES peak's position is the energy needed to remove an electron from a specific subshell; its height is roughly proportional to that subshell's electron count.
- Photon energy follows E = hv and equals the electron's binding energy plus its ejected kinetic energy.
ex.cpl: Confusing binding energy order with orbital filling order; a subshell with higher binding energy is held more tightly and closer to the nucleus, which is not necessarily the last subshell filled by the Aufbau principle.
ex.hp:
1. Match peak positions and relative heights to an element's electron configuration.
2. Explain binding-energy differences by distance from the nucleus and shielding.
3. Do not explain them by the order subshells were filled.
ex.pb: Head to practice and, on every PES question, sum the peak heights to get total electron count first, then match that configuration to an element before making any claim about binding energy order.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Count the peaks and compare their heights to find subshell electron counts, then match the pattern to an element's configuration.
How points are lost: Confusing binding energy order with orbital filling order.
ex.title: Photoelectron Spectroscopy
ex.wsu:
- PES reads the Topic 1.5 configuration rules directly off real data.
- Core electrons, closer to the nucleus and less shielded, always need more energy to remove than valence electrons, whichever subshell Aufbau filled last.

ex.am: For a trend question, choose whichever Coulombic factor actually differs between the two atoms or ions being compared, effective nuclear charge, distance from the nucleus, or shielding, and use only that factor to justify the direction of the trend.
ex.core:
- Periodic position reflects recurring electron-configuration patterns; ionization energy, radius, electron affinity and electronegativity trends follow from Coulomb's law, shielding and effective nuclear charge.
- Excluded from the AP Exam: aufbau-exception configurations (chromium, copper); the standard filling order applies wherever trends are tested.
ex.cpl: Correctly stating the direction of a trend, such as ionization energy increases across a period, without explaining why through effective nuclear charge and shielding; an unsupported direction claim does not earn the explanation point.
ex.hp:
1. Explain the trend with effective nuclear charge and distance from the nucleus or shielding.
2. Never just name the trend's direction.
3. Use that reasoning to make a specific comparison or estimate when exact data isn't given.
ex.pb: Go to practice and, before stating any periodic-trend direction, name which Coulomb's-law factor -- nuclear charge, distance, or shielding -- actually differs between the two atoms being compared.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Pick the Coulombic factor that actually differs (effective nuclear charge, distance or shielding) and justify the trend with it alone.
How points are lost: Stating the trend direction without explaining it through effective nuclear charge and shielding.
ex.title: Periodic Trends
ex.wsu:
- Trends let you predict or estimate a property for an unfamiliar element from its position alone.
- This reasoning is tested throughout the exam: the same Coulomb's-law logic reappears whenever a later unit compares or estimates a property.

ex.am: For common main-group ions, count valence electrons from the group number, determine how many electrons must be gained or lost to reach a noble-gas configuration, and use that number as the ion's typical charge.
ex.core:
- Bonding depends on how valence electrons interact with the nucleus; same-column elements form analogous compounds.
- Typical ionic charge follows from valence electron count and position, and total charge must balance to zero.
- NaCl predicts KCl (same column as Na), but not CaCl: Ca loses two electrons for 2+, so CaCl2 balances and CaCl does not.
ex.cpl: Guessing or misremembering an ionic charge instead of deriving it from valence electron count and group position, or proposing a compound formula whose total positive and negative charge does not balance to zero.
ex.hp:
1. Derive an ion's typical charge from its group number or valence-electron count.
2. Build a formula whose total positive and negative charge sums to zero.
3. Use same-column analogies, but never assume elements from different groups share a charge.
ex.pb: Return to practice and, on every ionic-formula question, derive each ion's charge from group number first, then check that the formula's total charge actually sums to zero before finalizing it.
ex.qt:
The answer move: For main-group ions, count valence electrons from the group, find the gain or loss to reach a noble-gas configuration, and use that as the charge.
How points are lost: Guessing an ionic charge, or writing a formula whose charges do not balance to zero.
ex.title: Valence Electrons and Ionic Compounds
ex.wsu:
- This sets up bonding and compound formation for Unit 2.
- From periodic position and the zero-total-charge requirement alone, you can predict a formula or analogous compound for an element you haven't seen.

w.q: A student weighs out 3.42 g of glucose (C6H12O6, molar mass 180.16 g/mol) and needs the number of glucose molecules in that mass before starting a titration calculation.
w.strong:
n = m/M = 3.42 g / 180.16 g/mol ~ 0.01898 mol.

Multiplying by Avogadro's number gives the particle count: 0.01898 mol x 6.022x10^23/mol ~ 1.14x10^22 glucose molecules.

Molar mass, not Avogadro's number, converts mass to moles; Avogadro's number only converts moles to particle count.
w.weak: n = 3.42 g / 6.022x10^23 = 5.68x10^-24 mol, so that's the number of molecules.

w.q: Magnesium's natural sample shows three mass-spectrum peaks: Mg-24 (mass 23.985 amu, 78.99% abundance), Mg-25 (24.986 amu, 10.00%), and Mg-26 (25.983 amu, 11.01%). Calculate the average atomic mass, then explain what makes Mg-25 one amu heavier than Mg-24.
w.strong:
| Isotope | Mass (amu) | Abundance | Product |
| Mg-24 | 23.985 | 0.7899 | 18.945 |
| Mg-25 | 24.986 | 0.1000 | 2.499 |
| Mg-26 | 25.983 | 0.1101 | 2.861 |

Sum ~ 24.31 amu, matching magnesium's periodic-table mass of 24.305.

Mg-24 and Mg-25 both have 12 protons (defining the element) and 12 electrons (neutral atom); the one-amu difference comes from Mg-25's one additional neutron.
w.weak: Average mass ~ 24.3 amu, and Mg-25 is heavier than Mg-24 because it has one more electron.

w.q: A compound is 40.0% C, 6.71% H, and 53.3% O by mass, with a molar mass of about 180 g/mol. Find its molecular formula.
w.strong:
The mole ratio C:H:O = 3.33:6.66:3.33 reduces to 1:2:1, giving empirical formula CH2O with empirical mass 12.01+2(1.008)+16.00 ~ 30.03 g/mol.

The actual molar mass (180 g/mol) is about 180.16/30.03 ~ 6 times the empirical mass, so the molecular formula is (CH2O)x6 = C6H12O6, not CH2O.

The empirical formula alone under-answers a molecular-formula question.
w.weak: Assuming 100 g: C = 40.0/12.01 = 3.33 mol, H = 6.71/1.008 = 6.66 mol, O = 53.3/16.00 = 3.33 mol. Dividing by the smallest value gives C1H2O1, so the formula is CH2O.

w.q: A clear liquid sold under one label gives Sample A: 11.2% H, 88.8% O by mass. A bottle from a different batch of the same product gives Sample B: 9.5% H, 90.5% O by mass. Is this product a pure substance?
w.strong:
| Sample | % H | % O |
| Water (H2O), fixed ratio | 11.19 | 88.81 |
| Sample A | 11.2 | 88.8 |
| Sample B | 9.5 | 90.5 |

Sample A matches that ratio, but Sample B does not: a pure substance's composition ratio cannot vary between samples.

Because the ratio changed between bottles, at least one sample is not the pure substance claimed; appearance (both being clear liquids) provides no evidence either way.
w.weak: Both samples are clear liquids that look identical, so this is a pure substance.

w.q: Write the ground-state electron configuration for sulfur (S, Z=16) and aluminum (Al, Z=13), and use those configurations to explain why sulfur has a higher first ionization energy than aluminum.
w.strong:
S: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4. Al: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p1.

| Factor | S | Al |
| Nuclear charge | +16 | +13 |
| Valence shell | n = 3 | n = 3 |
| Core electrons (shielding) | 10 | 10 |

The distance and shielding are about the same, but sulfur's nuclear charge is larger. By Coulomb's law the attraction on its valence electrons is stronger, so more energy is needed to remove one: sulfur's first ionization energy is higher.
w.weak: S: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4, Al: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p1. Sulfur has a higher ionization energy because it is farther to the right on the periodic table.

w.q: An unlabeled PES spectrum shows four peaks with relative heights, ordered from highest binding energy to lowest, of 2 : 2 : 6 : 2. Identify the element and justify the identification using the peak heights.
w.strong:
| Peak height | Subshell |
| 2 | 1s |
| 2 | 2s |
| 6 | 2p |
| 2 | 3s |

Heights 2:2:6:2 are electron counts: 2+2+6+2 = 12 total electrons, 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2, so magnesium (Z=12).

The highest-binding-energy peak (height 2) is 1s because 1s electrons sit closest to the nucleus and are least shielded, not because 1s was filled first or last. Binding-energy order and Aufbau filling order are different orderings.
w.weak: The highest-binding-energy peak must be the 3s peak, since 3s is one of the last subshells filled by the Aufbau principle.

w.q: Explain why the first ionization energy of chlorine (Cl, Z=17) is greater than that of sulfur (S, Z=16), even though chlorine has one more electron in the same 3p subshell.
w.strong:
Cl and S are in the same period, so their valence electrons sit at a similar distance from the nucleus with similar shielding from the same core configuration.

Chlorine has one more proton (Z=17 vs. 16), so greater effective nuclear charge. By Coulomb's law, a larger nuclear charge over a similar radius gives a stronger attraction on the valence electrons, so removing one from chlorine requires more energy.

The direction of the trend follows from this charge difference, not from the trend's name.
w.weak: Chlorine has a higher ionization energy than sulfur because ionization energy increases across a period.

w.q: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is a known ionic compound. Predict the formula of the compound formed between calcium and chlorine, using periodic position and valence-electron count.
w.strong:
| Element | Group | Reaches noble-gas configuration by | Typical charge |
| Ca | 2 | losing 2 valence electrons | 2+ |
| Cl | 17 | gaining 1 electron | 1- |

Balancing total charge to zero requires two Cl- ions for every Ca2+ ion, giving CaCl2.

The same-column analogy to NaCl breaks down because calcium's group, and therefore its charge, is different from sodium's.
w.weak: Calcium is near sodium on the periodic table, so the compound is probably CaCl, like NaCl.
